analysis.one_liner: Dedicates a 3.8% tax on high earners' investment and business income to Medicare.
analysis.headline: Referred to the House Ways and Means Committee in January 2025, the bill has received no hearing, markup, or floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill raises money for Medicare Part A, the hospital insurance program, by expanding a 3.8% tax that currently applies to investment income of households earning over $200,000. It would apply that tax to the business income of people earning over $400,000 ($500,000 for couples), closing the gap where high-income owners of companies organized as partnerships or S corporations pay no Medicare tax on that income. It also directs the tax's revenue into the Medicare hospital trust fund, which is projected to face a funding shortfall.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries and future retirees, because the bill channels new revenue into the Medicare Hospital Insurance Trust Fund that pays hospital bills for about 68 million people. It also modestly levels the playing field between salaried workers, who pay Medicare taxes on all their wages, and high-earning business owners, who currently avoid the 3.8% tax on income passed through their firms.

how_it_helps.text: Directs all revenue from the net investment income tax into the Federal Hospital Insurance Trust Fund, which finances Medicare Part A hospital care.
Applies the 3.8% tax to the greater of investment income or business income for individuals earning over $400,000 ($500,000 for joint filers), instead of only to investment income.
Closes exclusions that currently let high-income owners of partnerships and S corporations keep active business income out of the tax, and ends the exclusion of working-capital investment income.
Disallows net operating losses from reducing the tax and includes certain foreign-sourced income, broadening the base.

analysis.who_pays: Individuals with income above $400,000 ($500,000 for couples), estates, and trusts, especially owners of partnerships and S corporations who would pay the 3.8% tax on business income they currently exclude. The bill phases in the increase gradually for those taxpayers.

drawbacks.text: It is a tax increase on people earning over $400,000 who own businesses, and opponents argue that raising taxes on pass-through business income can reduce investment and hiring; the bill softens the blow with a phase-in that caps how fast the increase applies.
The bill strengthens only Medicare Part A's hospital trust fund; it does nothing about other Medicare financing pressures or health costs generally.

Because the threshold starts at $400,000 and phases in over $100,000 of excess income, the tax reaches far fewer high earners than the existing $200,000 investment-income threshold, limiting how much revenue it raises relative to Medicare's shortfall.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For Medicare beneficiaries, the benefit is a steadier funding stream for the hospital insurance program many rely on, paid for by the top fraction of earners. The main cost falls on a narrow, high-income group, and the phase-in and $400,000 floor keep the burden limited — though those limits also limit the revenue. The strongest honest objection is not that the beneficiaries don't deserve help, but that a tax reaching so few filers may close only a slice of Medicare's funding gap.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced, and no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled since.

narrative.text: Representative Lloyd Doggett introduced the bill on January 22, 2025 with 43 original Democratic cosponsors.
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
A total of 57 House Democrats had signed on as cosponsors; no Republicans did.
As of the latest action record, the committee has taken no further steps on the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, high-income business owners and investors who would have paid the expanded tax are better off, because the bill sits without committee action and the Republican-controlled committee has not moved it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners who would have paid the tax

for.name: Lloyd Doggett
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 43 original cosponsors from his party.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote scheduled in the months since introduction.

sides.party_line_note: All 58 initial supporters were House Democrats (57 of 217 cosponsored), and no Republican signed on; the committee that controls the bill's fate has a Republican majority.

industries.industry: High-income owners of partnerships and S corporations
industries.note: The bill would apply the 3.8% Medicare tax to active business income above $400,000 in earnings, income these owners currently keep out of the tax while salaried workers pay Medicare taxes on all their wages. Their savings come at the Medicare trust fund's expense.

industries.industry: Private investment funds and their managers
industries.note: Broadening the tax base to more business and foreign income, and disallowing operating losses as offsets, would raise taxes on fund income and carried returns flowing through partnerships.
New revenue dedicated to the Hospital Insurance Trust Fund supports the program that pays hospitals for treating Medicare patients, reducing payment uncertainty when the fund faces shortfalls.

analysis.trajectory: A tax increase bill with no Republican cosponsors referred to the tax-writing committee under a Republican majority very rarely advances; the most likely path is that it stays in committee and expires at the end of this Congress without a vote.
